p01: For two hundred twenty years, Japan locked its doors.
p02: Sneak out, and the punishment was death. Come back, and it was death again.
p03: Then four black ships arrived, and within twenty-three years, the samurai lost their swords.
p04: This is Japan, the Land of the Rising Sun.
p05: It has fourteen thousand one hundred twenty-five islands, double what it counted until twenty twenty-three.
p06: Here is how the doors closed, how they burst open, and which one is still waiting for you.
p07: So why lock them? Historians say the shogun wanted to cut off Spanish and Portuguese influence.
p08: From sixteen thirty-three to sixteen thirty-nine, edicts banned Japanese ships from sailing abroad.
p09: But Japan was never fully sealed. On Dejima, a fan-shaped island just one hundred twenty meters long, the Dutch were allowed to trade.
p10: Through it flowed Dutch books and medicine. Japanese scholars called it Dutch learning.
p11: Two doctors spent three years translating a single Dutch anatomy book.
p12: Then, on July eighth, eighteen fifty-three, four warships entered the bay at Edo, today's Tokyo.
p13: No sails. Only black smoke. People thought they were giant dragons puffing smoke.
p14: Commodore Perry handed over a letter, promised to return, and came back with a bigger fleet.
p15: In March eighteen fifty-four, Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa, opening two ports to American ships.
p16: Signed under threat of force, it ended about two hundred twenty years of seclusion.
p17: What followed was one of the fastest national makeovers in modern history.
p18: In eighteen sixty-eight, samurai loyalists seized the palace in Kyoto and restored a fifteen-year-old emperor, Meiji.
p19: Within three years, the old feudal domains were gone, replaced by prefectures.
p20: In eighteen seventy-two, the first railway opened, twenty-nine kilometers from Tokyo to Yokohama.
p21: And here is the twist. The leaders of this revolution were samurai, and they abolished the samurai.
p22: Their stipends ended in eighteen seventy-three. In eighteen seventy-six, they lost the right to carry swords in public.
p23: In eighteen seventy-seven, about fifteen thousand former samurai rebelled. They lost, and it was the last big uprising.
p24: But one door still shapes your trip. It is the genkan, the entrance where outdoor shoes stop.
p25: Japan draws a clear line between inside and outside. Never step onto the raised floor in your outdoor shoes.
p26: Slippers wait there. Take them off again before stepping onto tatami.
p27: In the bathroom, there is a second pair: toilet slippers. Walk out still wearing them, and you have made the classic tourist mistake.
p28: Outside, the rules continue. Public trash cans are rare, except at train stations and convenience stores, so carry your trash.
p29: And do not eat while walking. Sit down, or step out of the way.
p30: Japan locked its doors once. Today they open wide. Just know where to take off your shoes.
p31: That was Japan. Which country should we visit next? Tell me in the comments.
